name: Determinism and the denial of free will
plain_explanation: Nothing that happens could have happened otherwise; everything, mental and physical, follows from God's nature with the same necessity that 2 and 2 make 4.
precise_definition: The doctrine that all events, including human volitions, are governed by absolute logical necessity, so that chance and free will in the ordinary sense do not exist.
why_it_mattered: It creates the central puzzle of the chapter: how sin and evil can be meaningfully spoken of if everything is decreed by God and is, in that sense, 'good.'
historical_origin: A consequence Spinoza draws directly from his substance monism: since there is only one wholly positive Being, its acts cannot fail to occur as they do.
examples: Spinoza's answer to critics who asked whether it was 'good' that Nero killed his mother or that Adam ate the apple: what was positive in these acts was good, only the negative aspect (visible only from a finite viewpoint) appeared as evil.
objections: Contemporary critics pointed out this cannot be reconciled with the orthodox doctrine of sin and damnation.
Russell himself argues each act of cruelty is 'eternally a part of the universe' and does not become good by being absorbed into a supposed harmonious whole.
competing_positions: Christian doctrines of free will, sin, and damnation
connection_to_politics_or_religion: The rejection of free will was one of the chief reasons Spinoza was accused of impiety and atheism by his contemporaries.
